Effect of the compound used as a 
nitrogen source on Cherry Belle radish 
(Raphanus sativus) plant growth 
Plant the Moon Challenge | Spring 2023 | Professional/Undergraduate Division 
 
Minnesota West Bluejays | Team # 12926 
Minnesota West Community & Technical College 
Worthington, MN 
 
Selam Alemayehu, Julian Bennett, Brandon Berghorst, Leidy Chavez Martin, Devaughn Demus, 
Taya Denroche, Irma Hernandez, Antonio Heser-Leiva, Christian Lopez, Dylan Markus, Arlene 
Martinez Cambara, Irving Mendez, Emmot Nathan, Aaliyah Petersen, Taylor Pronto, Deante 
Porter, Lolita Ramirez Velasquez, Omar Robles, Simon Spittle, Paul Troe, Vant Tucker, 
Du’Vaughn Williams, Dr. Tyler Wadzinski, and Heidi Tarus 
Advised by Heidi Tarus 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
Grant Funded by NASA’s Minnesota Space Grant Consortium

P a g e | 1 
 
Introduction 
As humans on Earth look towards future colonization of celestial bodies, we must be 
able to address the basic needs of colonizing humans including access to protective shelter, 
clean and safe water, and nutritious food. This project focuses on addressing the human need 
of access to nutritious food that can be grown on the Moon. In order for plants to be grown for 
food, they need access to water and essential nutrients including potassium, phosphorus, and 
nitrogen. Prior studies show that most plant essential nutrients are available in the composition 
of lunar regolith with the exception of useful nitrogen (Wamelink et al., 2014). Therefore, this 
study focuses on the most efficient source of nitrogen needed to allow plants to grow while 
reducing the amount of payload required on a spacecraft. Nitrogen is an essential 
macronutrient for plants and is used in the synthesis of proteins, nucleic acids, and some 
vitamins needed for growth (Clark et al., 2018). The main driving question for this project is to 
discover the trade-off between limiting the mass of nitrogen fertilizers brought to the moon 
while producing the highest yield of nutrient rich crops needed to feed individuals living on the 
moon. 
Theory 
The nitrogen sources tested (independent variable) were calcium nitrate tetrahydrate 
(Ca(NO3)2∙4H2O), ammonium nitrate (NH4NO3), and urea (CO(NH2)2). The three nitrogen sources 
have different molar masses and nitrogen percent compositions. They also fall into different 
parts of the nitrogen cycle, which makes comparing the trade-off between reducing the mass 
added to the spacecraft and the success of plant growth an important question. Calcium nitrate 
tetrahydrate has the lowest percent composition of nitrogen, requiring 8.4 g of compound per 
gram of nitrogen delivered. The nitrogen in calcium nitrate tetrahydrate is available

P a g e | 2 
 
immediately to plants in the nitrate form; however, nitrate is water soluble and thus 
susceptible to leaching which is a major cause of nitrogen loss in soil. Ammonium nitrate has a 
higher percent composition of nitrogen and requires 2.9 g of compound per gram of nitrogen 
delivered. Ammonium nitrate provides a combination of 50% nitrate which is usable to plants 
right away and 50% ammonium which must be fixed by nitrogen fixing bacteria to nitrate 
before it is usable by plants (Isleib, 2017). Therefore, ammonium nitrate is a good source of 
short-term and long-term nitrogen. Urea has the highest mass percent of nitrogen and only 
requires 2.1 g of compound per gram of nitrogen delivered, which makes it the most preferred 
nitrogen source in regard to reducing rocket payload mass. However, urea must go through a 
three-step process where it is converted to ammonia, then ammonium, and then nitrate before 
plants can use it (Mengel n.d). Similar to nitrate, urea is water soluble prior to being converted, 
making it susceptible to leaching. An additional benefit of urea is that it can be locally sourced 
and extracted from urine produced by individuals living on the moon. Since the calcium nitrate 
tetrahydrate and the ammonium nitrate nitrogen sources being used in this experiment need 
to be fixed by nitrogen fixing bacteria the lunar soil will be amended with 25% top soil which 
will contain the nitrogen fixing bacteria needed for this process to occur. 
The team decided to plant Cherry Belle radishes (Raphanus sativus) because they are 
container friendly, have a fast germination time of four to six days with 22 days to harvest, and 
retain their taste quality for a long time after harvest to prevent food waste. The nutritional 
value of Cherry Belle radish bulbs is high. According to the U.S. Department of Agriculture 
(2019), one medium (3/4” – 1” diameter) cherry belle radish bulb (4.5g) contains 0.72 calories, 
0.031g of protein, 0.072g of fiber, 0.153g of carbohydrate, and 0.004g of fat. In addition, R.

P a g e | 3 
 
sativus are an excellent source of many essential vitamins and minerals for humans including 
vitamin C, Vitamin B6, riboflavin, niacin, thiamine, folate, potassium, iron, manganese, and 
calcium (Begum, 2022). Not only are the radish bulbs able to be used for food, but so are the 
stems, leaves, and roots, making it an efficient plant to produce. R. sativus have many uses in 
foods like salads, chicken sandwiches, and many other foods. R. sativus also has medicinal value 
and can be used as an antibacterial when you extract its alcohol (Perera, 2022). Due to the 
plant choice by the team, a second soil amendment of 25% vermiculite was be added. 
Vermiculite is a lightweight magnesium-aluminum-iron silicate that is used for water and 
nutrient retention (Gwmag, 2021). In addition, vermiculite can help aerate the soil to reduce 
the amount of compaction that occurs when the lunar regolith is watered. Making sure the soil 
is not compact is important radish bulbs will only develop in loose soil which allows the roots to 
thicken into bulbs (Grant, 2021). 
The data collected in the experiment (dependent variables) will include the primordial 
leaf emergence for germination rate, plant height, final leaf surface area, radish bulb mass, and 
pH of the pots. Past studies show that R. sativus plant height, final leaf surface area, and radish 
bulb mass are directly related to the amount of nitrogen added to the soil (Jiliani et al, 2010 and 
Yousaf et al, 2021). Therefore, we conclude that the listed dependent variables will be good 
proxies to show nitrogen uptake in the treatment groups. 
We hypothesized that (1) the nitrogen source will not influence the germination 
(primordial leaf emergence) rate of the R. sativus plants, (2) the R. sativus plants grown in pots 
containing a nitrogen source will produce a higher leaf height growth rate, a larger leaf surface 
area, and the largest bulb compared to the control group and (3) out of the three nitrogen

P a g e | 4 
 
sources being tested, ammonium nitrate (NH4NO3) will produce the highest leaf height growth 
rate, the largest leaf surface area, and the largest bulbs due to the ability of ammonium nitrate 
to provide both fast acting short-term nitrate and slower acting long-term nitrate that goes 
through fixation. 
Experiment & Measurement Methods 
Initial Set-Up 
The independent variable for this experiment was the type of nitrogen-containing 
compound used as a nitrogen source. The experimental set-up included four treatments, (1) 
control (no nitrogen source), (2) calcium nitrate tetrahydrate, (3) ammonium nitrate, and (4) 
urea with each treatment having 8 replicates (Figure 1). Each pot (7cm x 7cm x 7.7cm) 
contained the same soil composition of 25% top soil, 25% vermiculite, and 50% lunar regolith 
by volume. Rational for this soil mixture is addressed in the theory section above. Each nitrogen 
source was weighed as a pure solid and then mixed into the soil to achieve the recommended 
fertilizing loading rate of 0.5 lb N per 1000 ft2 (Swift & Hammond, 2020; Kokemuller 2016; Table 
1). Each pot was watered with 25ml of water. 
The larger team of 22 students formed eight sub-teams that contained one to three 
students per team. Each sub-team was responsible for one pot per treatment. The pots were 
identified by a colored popsicle stick placed in the back of the pot with the team’s name written 
on it. The eight team names were Tarus, DIL, DO, ATT, ND, Agricultural Space Scientists (A.S.S.), 
I.M., and Ambiguity. The team planted each treatment pot with 3 Burpee Cherry Belle radish 
(Raphanus sativus; Packed for 2023, Lot 7) seeds and watered with 25ml of tap water. Over the 
course of the eight-week grow period, the set-up was kept indoors with a temperature of 22°C

P a g e | 5 
 
with the set of pots placed under a grow light containing 2-18” GE plant and aquarium bulbs on 
a 12-hour light: 12-hour dark timer. The grow light was placed 12 cm from the top of the pots 
(Figure Set 1).

Plant Care 
Each pot was top watered with 25ml of distilled water on Tuesday and Thursday each 
week during the grow period. All pots were watered on the same schedule independent of the 
presence of seedling or no seedlings. According to the seed packet, the R. sativus should be 
thinned to be at least 5.08 cm (two inches) apart; therefore, as the pots are 7cm in width, the 
plants were thinned to one seedling on March 9, 2023 by keeping the tallest plant in the pot.

P a g e | 7 
 
Thinning is a common practice in gardening and was done to give the tallest (strongest) 
seedling in each pot the best chance to grow. The plants were kept in the same room through 
the duration of the experiment and were moved away for the light source for a maximum of 30 
minutes on Thursday at 1pm to take measurements and then replaced back in the same 
location after measuring. 
Measurements 
 The dependent variables for this experiment were primordial leaf emergence for 
germination rate, plant height, final leaf surface area, radish bulb mass, and pH of the pots. 
Primordial leaf emergence was used to collect data on germination rate of the plants. 
Germination rate was collected once by visually observing of the number of germinated seeds 
14 days after planting. The soil pH measurements and plant height measurement were 
collected by sub-team members once a week each on Thursday using the soil pH meter sent 
with the lunar regolith an a 15-cm ruler. Leaf surface area was collected during the final week 
on Tuesday, April 4, 2023 using the LeafByte App, https://zoegp.science/leafbyte. This was 
done by holding up a scale (a white piece of paper with four black dots in the shape of a square) 
behind the leaf, taking a picture with a smart phone, identifying the scale, and having the app 
calculate the square centimeters of the leaf (Image Set 2).

Final radish bulb size data was collected by carefully removing the soil out of the pots by 
pouring the soil into a black plastic growing tray, removing the plants from the soil in the tray, 
washing off excess soil from the roots, and placing the plants on a paper towel labeled with the 
treatment and the popsicle stick containing the team name. Unfortunately, radish bulbs did not 
develop in the soil (Appendix B: Photos) so no quantitative data was collected on radish size. 
Images were taken of the plants to document the qualitative results. 
In addition, a top-view and side-view picture of the entire set-up was taken twice a 
week on Tuesday and Thursday after watering the pots (Appendix B: Photos). Records of the 
data collected was kept on paper next to the set up and was entered each week into a 
Microsoft Excel spreadsheet each week for data analysis.

Analysis & Results 
Data for each sub-team was written down on paper data collection sheets and entered 
into a Microsoft Excel spreadsheet each week. The paper data collection sheets were stored in 
the biology lab and electronic copies of the data was stored on Tarus’ laptop computer. The 
data was organized and graphed using Microsoft Excel. Statistical tests for the means, standard 
errors, rates using linear fit, Shapiro-Wilk tests for normality, Kruskal Wallis H tests, and ANOVA 
tests were performed using the free online website Statistics Kingdom 
(https://www.statskingdom.com/). 
Soil pH & Germination Rate 
The soil pH of each pot did not change over the course of the eight weeks and stayed at 
a pH of 8 (Appendix A Table 5). Because the pH did not change over time statistical analysis was 
not done on this data. The germination (primordial leaf emergence) data collected on day 14 
shows that the seeds had a mean ± standard error germination rate of 50% ± 16% in the control 
group, 50% ± 13% in the calcium nitrate tetrahydrate group, 58% ± 11% in the ammonium 
nitrate group and 62% ± 9% in the urea group (Appendix A Table 2 and Figure 2).

P a g e | 10 
 
Figure 2. Box plot with whiskers showing the effect of the compound used as a nitrogen 
source on average germination rate (primordial leaf emergence) at 14 days after planting on 
March 2, 2024. Each treatment group contained eight pots (N = 8) where three seeds were 
planted per pot. 
 
 
A Shapiro-Wilk tests showed a significance departure from the normality for the control 
group, W(8) = .799, p = .035, but did not showed a significance departure from the normality 
for the calcium nitrate tetrahydrate group, W(8) = .897, p = .297, the ammonium nitrate group, 
W(8) = .918, p = .456, or for the urea group, W(8) = .835, p = .075. Because the data did not 
show normality for all four groups, a Kruskal-Wallis H test was used to analyze the between 
group data. The Kruskal-Wallis H test indicated that there was a non-significant difference in 
the germination rate between the four groups, χ2(3) = 0.53, p = .912, with a mean rank score of

P a g e | 11 
 
15.5 for the control group, 15.25 for the calcium nitrate tetrahydrate group, 17.19 for the 
ammonium nitrate group, 18.06 for the urea group. 
Plant Height Growth Rate 
Plant height was measured each week and the data was analyzed using a linear 
regression model to show plant height growth over the grow period. The linear regression 
model calculated the average rate of plant height growth during the measurement period was 
0.05082 cm/day for the control group (X predicted Y, R2 = .59, F(1,5) = 7.23, p = .043), 0.1393 
cm/day for the calcium nitrate tetrahydrate group (X predicted Y, R2 = .92, F(1,5) = 56.68, p < 
.001), 0.1356 cm/day for the ammonium nitrate group (X predicted Y, R2 = .91, F(1,5) = 48.13, p 
< .001.), and 0.1366 cm/day for the urea group (X predicted Y, R2 = .86, F(1,5) = 31.5, p = .002.; 
Appendix A Table 3 and Figure 3).

Shapiro-Wilk tests did not showed a significance departure from the normality for plant 
height growth rate in the control group, W(5) = .937, p = .808, the calcium nitrate tetrahydrate 
group, W(5) = .832, p = .178, the ammonium nitrate group, W(7) = .842, p = .116, or the urea 
group, W(8) = .848, p = .100. Because the data show normal distribution, a one-way ANOVA test 
was used to analyze the between group data. 
 
A one-way ANOVA was performed to compared the effect of the compound 
used as a nitrogen source on plant height growth rate. The test revealed that there was a 
statistically significant difference in the plant height growth rate between at least two groups 
(F(3,21)= [8.1784], p = 0.0008508). Tukey’s HSD Test for multiple comparisons found that the 
mean value of plant height growth rate was significantly different between the control and the 
calcium nitrate tetrahydrate group (p = 0.003207, 95% C.I. = [0.02713, 0.1416]), the control and 
the ammonium nitrate group (p = 0.001572, 95% C.I. = [0.03052, 0.1411]), and the control and 
the urea group (p = 0.003207, 95% C.I. = [0.02713, 0.0.06135]). There was no statistically 
significant difference in plant height growth rate between the calcium nitrate tetrahydrate and 
ammonium nitrate group (p=0.9978), the calcium nitrate tetrahydrate and urea group 
(p=0.9991) or between the ammonium nitrate and urea group (p=0.999).

Final Leaf Surface Area 
The final leaf surface area data collected on day 47 shows that the plants in the control 
group had a mean ± standard error leaf surface area of 5.715 ± 0.86 cm2 in the control group, 
27.489 ± 4.64 cm2 for the calcium nitrate tetrahydrate group, 31.543 ± 3.49 cm2 for the 
ammonium nitrate group had, and 39.223 ± 5.38 cm2 for urea group (Appendix A Table 4 and 
Figure 4).

P a g e | 14 
 
Figure 4. Box plot with whiskers showing the effect of the compound used as a nitrogen source on 
final leaf surface area (cm2). 
 
 
 
A Shapiro-Wilk tests showed a significance departure from the normality for the urea 
group, W(7) = .692, p = .007, but did not showed a significance departure from the normality 
for the control group, W(5) = .909, p = .576, the calcium nitrate tetrahydrate group, W(5) = 
.899, p = .502, or the ammonium nitrate group, W(7) = .865, p = .187. Because the data did not 
show normality for all four groups, a Kruskal-Wallis H test was used to analyze the between 
group data. The Kruskal-Wallis H test indicated that there is a significant difference in the final 
leaf surface area between the different groups, χ2(3) = 12.63, p = .005, with a mean rank score 
of 3.6 for the control group, 11.8 for the calcium nitrate tetrahydrate group, 13.71 for the

P a g e | 15 
 
ammonium nitrate group, 18.14 for the urea group. The Post-Hoc Dunn's test using a 
Bonferroni corrected alpha of 0.0083 indicated that the mean rank of the between the control 
group and the urea group is significantly different. 
Final Radish Bulb Mass 
As discussed in the measurement methods section radish bulbs did not develop in the 
soil (Appendix B: Photos) so no quantitative data was collected on radish bulb size. Images were 
taken of the plants to document the qualitative results. After viewing the images, it was noticed 
that two plants in the ammonium nitrate group show slight swelling in the area where the 
radish bulbs are supposed to develop (Image Set 3); regrettably, the plants were disposed of 
prior to this discovery and thus quantitative data was not collected. 
Discussion & Conclusion 
 We hypothesized that (1) the nitrogen source will not influence the germination 
(primordial leaf emergence) rate of the R. sativus plants, (2) the R. sativus plants grown in pots

ammonium nitrate treatment showing swelling (black arrows) in the area where radish bulb 
development should take place.

P a g e | 16 
 
containing a nitrogen source will produce a higher leaf height growth rate, a larger leaf surface 
area, and the largest bulb compared to the control group and (3) out of the three nitrogen 
sources being tested, ammonium nitrate (NH4NO3) will produce the highest leaf height growth 
rate, the largest leaf surface area, and the largest bulbs due to the ability of ammonium nitrate 
to provide both fast acting short-term nitrate and slower acting long-term nitrate that goes 
through fixation. 
 
Data from the experiment supported the first hypothesis. There was no significant 
difference between the treatment groups and the primordial leaf germination rate. The main 
external factors that influence R. sativus germination rate are soil moisture, oxygen, 
temperature, seed viability, seed depth, pH, salinity and seed vitality (Anja & Felipe, 2021). The 
soil moisture, oxygen, and temperature were controlled in the experiment. The seed viability 
and seed vitality may have played a factor; however, all seeds were taken from the same seed 
packet. The pH of the pots stayed consistent through the experiment; however, salinity was not 
measured over the course of the experiment. The plants could have been planted as different 
seed depths since the experiment was done in sub-groups and seed depth was not mentioned 
during planting. 
 
Data from the experiment rejected the second and third hypothesis. Although all three 
the nitrogen sources produced a significantly higher height growth rate, only urea showed a 
significantly higher leaf surface area compared to the control. However, the urea group was not 
significantly different from the calcium nitrate tetrahydrate and ammonium nitrate groups 
which were not significantly different from the control group. The lack of significance could 
come from the small sample size in the experiment because the graph shows that the plants in

P a g e | 17 
 
the nitrogen compound treatment groups did have larger leaf surface areas compared to the 
control groups (Figure 4). Leaf surface area served as a proxy for nitrogen uptake since nitrogen 
plays an important role in the synthesis or chlorophyll and other enzymes important for 
photosynthesis which is the metabolic process that drives plant growth and yield (Koch 
Agronomic Services, n.d.). As mentioned in the results, radish bulbs did not develop except for 
slight swelling on two of the plants in the ammonium nitrate treatment. Reasons why radish 
bulbs may not have developed was because the soil was too compact even with the addition of 
vermiculate and the possibility of adding too much nitrogen to the soil which promotes the 
growth of the leafy tops (Grant, 2021). The team suggest adding a different amendment that 
would reduce compaction of the soil to see if a different amendment would promote radish 
bulb formation. The team recommends adding peat moss, compost, manure, or earthworms to 
loosen the soil (Iannotti, 2021). 
The overall goal of the project was to find a nitrogen source that produced the best 
plant growth while reducing the payload on the spacecraft. Although radish bulbs did not 
develop, based on the data the team recommends the use of urea as a nitrogen source when 
growing R. sativus as urea is the most weight efficient nitrogen source tested in this 
experiment. In addition, the requirement to bring urea from Earth of the Moon may not be 
needed as urea can potentially be extracted from the urine of humans living on the Moon. 
Human typically produce 12 to 20 g of urea in urine over the course of 24-hours (Jacob, 2021). 
Depending on the number of humans and the nitrogen requirements of the plants being grown, 
this amount of urea could be sufficient to avoid bringing urea to the Moon. Investigations into 
the method and efficiency of urea extraction from human urine is needed.

P a g e | 18 
 
Future Research 
In addition, to future research discussed above the following areas are suggested for 
future research. The compounds used as a nitrogen source were added during the initial set-up, 
so experiments looking at the reapplication of nitrogen fertilizer and its influence Raphanus 
sativus plant growth should be investigated. This is especially significant for the calcium nitrate 
tetrahydrate and urea since these two compounds are susceptible to leeching quickly from the 
soil. Future experiments could involve comparing the nutritional content and quality of the R. 
sativus plants for each of the treatments which would allow the team to give a more informed 
recommendation as there could potentially be a tradeoff between payload the nutritional value 
and quality of the plants (Yousaf, 2021). In addition, nitrogen is important in building the 
enzyme ribulose-1-5-bisphosphate carboxylase-oxygenase (RuBisCO) which is the enzyme used 
during carbon fixation in the light-independent reaction during photosynthesis. A future study 
could measure the photosynthetic rate of the plants as a measure for nitrogen uptake in the 
plants. Finally, the team suggests replicating the set-up used during this experiment using a 
bigger sample size and using other plant species to see which nitrogen source would be best for 
growing other nutrient rich plants that could be used as a food source for humans on the 
Moon.
